checkpoints: An email carries two separate addressing layers, not one, and they serve completely different purposes.

The envelope layer: before content is even transferred, the SMTP session declares MAIL FROM and one RCPT TO per recipient, and this is the only layer the server uses to decide where the message actually goes.

The content layer: only after the envelope is settled does DATA carry headers like From/To/Cc, which are purely content rendered by the recipient's client and never consulted by the server for routing.
BCC mechanism: adding an address to BCC puts it into RCPT TO at the envelope layer so the server delivers to it, while deliberately keeping it out of the To/Cc headers inside DATA.
The teammate's confusion is exactly because they're reading only the displayed header layer, while the layer that actually decides delivery sits invisibly in the envelope.
SPF validates against the envelope MAIL FROM (the return-path), not the From header the user sees.
Consequence: a spoofer can set the From header to anyone while keeping a valid MAIL FROM, so a naive header-only SPF check won't catch that spoofing.
Most mail libraries auto-sync the envelope from the message's to/cc/bcc fields unless deliberately overridden, e.g. to set a distinct return-path for bounce handling.
Idempotency for this endpoint means calling the same request any number of times still produces exactly the effect of one send — no duplicate message, no duplicate charge.
It's mandatory, not a nice-to-have, because SMS is a costly, non-reversible side effect and network retries (client timeout, crashed process, k8s restart mid-request) can always happen.
The dangerous window is after the provider has accepted and sent the message but before the response reaches the client — a naive retry in that window replays the request and double-sends.

Standard pattern: the client attaches a unique idempotency key to the request; the server checks a fast key-value store first — a hit returns the cached message id, a miss calls the provider and then persists the id with a TTL.
The idempotency key must be generated by the client, never the server.
The client creates a UUID before the very first call, holds it in its own state, and reuses that exact same UUID for every retry of the same intent.
If the server generated the key instead, a lost first response leaves the client with no key to reuse, forcing its retry to be treated as a "new" request — an unsolvable duplication case.
The TTL bounds the practical dedup window (roughly 24h); after expiry, reusing the same key to send again is legitimate since the contract is one key per one send intent, not forever.

A userId read straight off a query string with no signature or session check is not authentication — it is a bare, enumerable value, so incrementing it to another user's id and hitting the same endpoint silently unsubscribes a stranger.

A trustworthy unsubscribe link is a server-signed, stateless token carrying userId, channel, category, and an expiry, computed with something like crypto.createHmac and verified using crypto.timingSafeEqual — never `===`, which leaks a byte of timing information per comparison — so the link needs no login yet cannot be forged or replayed past its exp.

A single boolean column on the user entity cannot represent per-channel, per-category consent — it forces "disable marketing SMS" and "disable transactional email" to be the same on/off bit instead of independent choices.

The fix for that granularity problem is a UserPreference row per (userId, channel, category) with a composite unique constraint, written through an idempotent upsert on those three columns, so flipping one preference touches exactly that pair and leaves every sibling channel/category untouched.

Marketing messages rest on consent and must be opt-outable, while OTPs and order confirmations rest on performance-of-contract obligations — gating both kinds of mail behind the same unsubscribed flag risks silently suppressing a login code because of an unrelated marketing opt-out click.

Because transactional messages are not consent-based, an unsubscribe endpoint should explicitly refuse to act on a transactional category — returning 400 Bad Request — rather than honoring the opt-out as if it applied.

Stamping deletedAt on the User row while the id and every UserPreference row remain intact is still personal-data processing, so it does not satisfy GDPR Article 17 erasure; genuine erasure means deleting the user row and all associated preference rows in one transaction, keeping at most a one-way-hashed audit entry as proof erasure occurred.

A still-valid unsubscribe token clicked after the underlying user has already been erased is an idempotent edge case: the endpoint should return 200 with nothing left to update rather than throw a 500 on a missing row.

Each `sendMail` call is a full SMTP session — connect, EHLO, AUTH, DATA — so awaiting it directly inside a request handler couples that request's latency, and its very availability, to the health of the mail relay.

In the register handler, `await this.mailService.sendWelcome(...)` sits between the user being created and the HTTP response, so a slow or unreachable SMTP relay makes an otherwise-successful signup hang or time out even though the account was already persisted.

The correct fix is enqueue-and-respond: the controller persists a job (e.g. `mailQueue.add('welcome', { userId, email, name })`) and returns immediately, while a separate worker/processor performs the actual SMTP send outside the request lifecycle, so request latency collapses to the queue-insert time.

The newsletter's `for...await` loop sends to ~10,000 recipients sequentially on a single non-pooled transporter, meaning the whole job runs for hours and every iteration re-pays SMTP connection/handshake overhead instead of reusing a connection.

Because the loop has no per-recipient tracking, a failure partway through (e.g. at recipient #5000) aborts the remaining recipients entirely and leaves no record of who was already sent, making the operation neither resumable nor auditable.

The bulk path should be restructured into one queued job per recipient (e.g. via `addBulk`), with the worker's concurrency and a rate limiter bounded to the relay's actual sending quota, protecting relay limits and sender reputation instead of hammering the relay unbounded.

Persisting per-recipient job state in the queue (e.g. Redis-backed) means a crash mid-run only loses in-flight jobs rather than the whole batch, and jobs can declare retry attempts with exponential backoff to recover automatically from transient SMTP failures.

Moving sends off the request path makes delivery eventual rather than synchronous, so the design needs a dead-letter path plus monitoring for exhausted-retry jobs, and any UI copy claiming an email was 'sent' must be changed to 'queued' since delivery is no longer guaranteed at response time.

A `queued` status from an SMS provider's send call only confirms the provider accepted the request into its own pipeline — it says nothing about whether the carrier actually delivered the message to the phone, since the real `sent → delivered/failed` outcome is decided later, out of band from the `create()` response.

A fixed-delay timer that resends an OTP whenever it fires, without checking delivery outcome, is a blind guess standing in for missing information: because most users read and type a code slower than the provider needs to deliver it, the timer routinely fires after the first message already arrived, producing a paid duplicate send on nearly every successful login.

When a message is genuinely failing (for example, carrier filtering on the sender ID), retrying it identically down the same route just pays for more guaranteed failures instead of solving the underlying delivery problem.

Registering the provider's status-callback webhook lets delivery state be pushed asynchronously as the message transitions `queued → sent → delivered/failed`; persisting that status per message (keyed by the provider's message id) gives the system a ground truth to react to instead of a clock.

Automatic resend should be driven exclusively by an observed `failed`/`undelivered` status from the webhook, never by elapsed time — this eliminates the duplicate-spend pattern because a message already marked delivered is never resent.

A user-visible "resend code" action needs to be separated from automatic delivery-failure resend and gated by its own cooldown window plus a persistent attempt cap, so that repeated manual taps still result in at most one real paid send once the cooldown clears.

After repeated delivery failures on the same route, the system should escalate laterally to a fallback — an alternate SMS route/regional provider, or a different channel such as email — rather than retrying the identical send a third time down a route that has already proven broken.

Keeping one idempotency key per logical send intent ensures that infrastructure-level retries (crashed workers, retried jobs) can never trigger a second paid send for what is conceptually the same OTP attempt.

Moving from a fixed timer to webhook-driven resend trades a small amount of latency (waiting on the provider's real signal) and added infrastructure (a callback endpoint and its own reliability) for near-elimination of duplicate spend — an acceptable trade for a channel that bills per message sent.

Correct behavior can be validated by simulating provider callbacks: a `delivered` callback should trigger no resend, a `failed` callback should trigger exactly one resend, and rapidly repeated clicks on the user-triggered resend endpoint should still be constrained by the cooldown and attempt cap.
Two-operation contract: `issue(identifier)` and `verify(identifier, code)`, each returning its own distinct response status (not a shared/generic response for both).

The keyspace uses two separate ephemeral keys per identifier — a code key (holds the current code, overwritten on every re-issue) and a distinct attempt-counter key (tracks failed tries) — each carrying its own TTL.
`issue()` normalizes the identifier (lowercased/trimmed) so that `verify()` later looks up the exact same key.
`verify()` gates on the attempt counter FIRST — once it's at the limit, it rejects immediately with a lockout response and doesn't even read the code key.
On success, `verify()` deletes BOTH the code key and the attempt key in the same step — single-use consumption plus a clean reset of the attempt budget for the next code.

CRUX: the attempt key is never touched by a re-issued code — only its own TTL clears it — explicitly defended as preventing an attacker who has burned attempts from resetting that budget just by requesting a fresh code.

On failure, `verify()` returns the exact same generic response regardless of cause (wrong code, expired, or never issued) — the API must not act as an oracle revealing which identifiers currently hold a live code.

Names at least one concrete, defensible trade-off — e.g. longer TTL helps a slow inbox but widens the attack window, a longer lockout protects harder but costs more support tickets, or counting only failed attempts (not every attempt) avoids punishing a user who mistypes then succeeds.
The core boundary is a single narrow exported service — `notify(recipient, category, payload)` — that every feature module injects; nothing else about messaging is visible to the caller.

Preference resolution lives inside the dispatcher: it looks up the preference row by the same composite key `(userId, channel, category)` used in the `UNIQUE(userId, channel, category)` schema, then fans out to whichever channels are enabled — putting the check in the dispatcher rather than the caller is the whole point, since a check living in the caller eventually gets forgotten.

Category semantics belong to the contract: the marketing category respects suppression (consent required, opt-out any time), while the transactional category (OTPs, order confirmations) is always-delivered based on legitimate interest/performance of contract.
The module refuses any attempt to mark a transactional category as suppressible — mirroring an API returning 400 Bad Request rather than silently honoring the opt-out.

Each channel (email, SMS) is a sealed submodule owning its own provider client — a MailService wrapping Nodemailer, a TwilioService wrapping the Twilio SDK — built once from config namespaced through ConfigModule; provider credentials and SDK types never cross this boundary, so swapping providers stays internal to the channel submodule.
Dispatch enqueues and returns immediately — delivery, retries, and status tracking belong to the channel worker, so caller latency is never coupled to SMTP or Twilio uptime.
Extensibility proof: adding a push channel means one new submodule plus one new channel value in the preference model, with no feature module changes required.

Trade-off to defend: this module becomes critical shared infrastructure needing its own SLO, and the rare need to await delivery gets an explicit, separately-named escape hatch rather than loosening the default fire-and-forget behavior.
TTL expiry — the key was written together with its own lifetime and vanished before the user got around to typing the code; that's expected behavior, not a bug.
Single-use — a successful verify deletes the key on the spot, so any replay attempt with the same code fails by design.

Re-request overwrite — every new send overwrites the stored code with a fresh TTL, so a user who taps "resend" and then types the code from the FIRST message will always fail even though that code still "looks right" in their inbox.

Un-normalized identifier — if the send path stores under a differently-cased or untrimmed key than the verify path reads, those are two entirely different keys in the store, and verification can never succeed until the identifier is lowercased and trimmed before becoming key material.

Diagnosis method: reproduce with a test identifier, list the matching keys and their remaining TTLs mid-flow, and log the exact key string each path derives — a mismatch shows up immediately as two different keys where there should only ever be one.

Test credentials hit the exact same API endpoint as usual, but the provider recognizes that AccountSid as a test one and returns a simulated response — no carrier is contacted, no handset receives anything, no charge is deducted (a magic number like `+15005550010` is meaningless outside that test environment) — so the dev pipeline "looks successful" not because the system is correct, but because the test environment never touches any of production's real failure layers.

First production failure layer — addressing: the recipient number must be E.164 (`+84901234567`); a local format like `0901234567` is globally ambiguous and gets rejected right at the validation layer with an invalid-number error, the earliest and most visible failure.

Second production failure layer — the carrier leg: the API accepting a request doesn't mean the message reaches a phone, since carriers in markets like Vietnam filter traffic from unregistered senders, requiring either a registered Sender ID with local telcos or a regional provider with a carrier agreement — the most silent failure, since the API still returns 201 as if nothing went wrong.

Third production failure layer — economics and observability: every real send now costs money and delivery happens asynchronously, so go-live needs a mechanism to track real delivery status rather than trusting an accepted-request response alone.
Go-live checklist (technical): swap credentials from test to live purely through configuration (no code change), and normalize phone numbers to E.164 right at the boundary before sending.
Go-live checklist (rollout): register the sender or pick the right regional route for the target market, and verify with a small live pilot before opening traffic at scale.
An OTP is ephemeral data with a fixed lifetime — created, used once, expired — a profile that maps directly onto an in-memory store's primitives.

On expiry: a single atomic set-with-expiry command writes the value and the lifetime together, avoiding a cleanup cron, an `expires_at` drifting out of sync, or a crash window leaving an "immortal" row behind in a table.

On counting attempts: a key-value store executes commands sequentially so incrementing the attempt counter is atomic and never races, while a database needs the full weight of transaction machinery to get the same guarantee.
On latency: this step sits right on the login hot path, and an in-memory operation completes in well under a millisecond.

Durability trade-off: a restart can drop the entire keyspace, but losing an OTP just means the user asks for a new one, so the system's weakest durability requirement lands on its fastest storage tier.
Reversal condition: if traffic were tiny, or if compliance demanded a durable audit trail of every code ever sent, the calculation could flip back toward the database.
